new_entities.name: Low-dose naltrexone for long COVID
new_entities.description: Off-label low-dose naltrexone used as a symptom-management treatment for long COVID or post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection.

new_entities.name: Symptom severity
new_entities.description: The overall intensity of symptoms reported by patients during follow-up.

edges.effect_quant: The strongest clinical signal is a 59-patient retrospective cohort in which off-label LDN use was associated with fewer symptoms and better functional status; in a separate long-COVID clinic survey, 58% of LDN users (45/77) rated it helpful.
edges.population: adults with long COVID or post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection
edges.mechanism: Low-dose naltrexone is hypothesized to dampen neuroinflammatory and innate-immune signaling and may also influence symptom amplification pathways relevant to fatigue, sleep, and pain. Those mechanisms are plausible for long COVID, but the current clinical evidence is still too observational and small to rule out expectancy effects or selection bias.
edges.summary: The strongest anchor is the small retrospective PASC cohort, where patients given low-dose naltrexone reported fewer symptoms and better function, and that signal is echoed by a clinic survey and a mechanistic study of restored TRPM3 ion-channel behavior. But none of this yet substitutes for randomized efficacy data, so the fairest current interpretation is contested and low-certainty rather than clearly beneficial.
edges.caveats: The controlled trial evidence is still pending, and the published long-COVID data are dominated by observational designs and mechanistic work. Patients offered LDN in specialty clinics may differ systematically from untreated patients, so the apparent benefit could be partly confounded by case selection, co-interventions, or regression toward the mean.
